description_full: Belden Inc. provides connection solutions to bring data infrastructure into alignment to unlock new possibilities for its customers. The company provides copper cable and connectivity solutions, fiber cable and connectivity solutions, interconnect panels, racks and enclosures, and signal extension and matrix switching systems for use in local area networks, data centers, access control, 5G, fiber to the home, and building automation applications. It also provides power, cooling, and airflow management products for mission-critical data center operations; and end-to-end fiber and copper network systems. It also serves commercial real estate, education, financial institutions, stadiums and venues, military installations, and broadband and wireless service providers, as well as data centers, government, healthcare, and hospitality sectors. In addition, the company offers network digitization and automation solutions; and products and solutions covering various aspects of data handling, including acquisition, transmission, orchestration, and management for applications in discrete automation, process automation, energy, and mass transit. It sells its products to distributors, end-users, installers, and original equipment manufacturers (OEMs). It operates in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia-Pacific. The company was formerly known as Belden CDT Inc. and changed its name to Belden Inc. in May 2007. Belden Inc. was founded in 1902 and is headquartered in Saint Louis, Missouri.

financial_summary: Belden Inc is a mid-cap technology business with a $3.8B market cap on $2.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 9% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 36%.

The business throws off $219M in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.49× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.0× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 7.3×.

Net dilution runs at 0.1% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 12% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.50x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+3.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 5% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 39% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 43% and a beta of 1.07, it moves roughly with the market.
About $43.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 50% in the 2020 crash, 25% in the 2022 bear market and 81% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 42% below its DCF fair value of $169, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 55%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $93.23 to $299 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/FCF 17.5 vs 25.4 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-6%).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.7% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $151 on average, 55% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 8.6%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.39).
It runs a 36% gross margin and converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.49x.
ROE of 19% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 4.7% of revenue on R&D and 1.1% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.0x net debt to EBITDA ($389.9M of cash against $1.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 7.3x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.4% over 3 years, 7.8% over 5 years and 1.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 12%).
At current returns, reinvesting 30% of profits supports about 4.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 21.3% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 5.0% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 15, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.6%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
The share count has shrunk 2.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 21 consecutive years, though it has been cut 2.5% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 15.2% of the float, 9.6 days to cover.
people: With about 8,000 employees, each generates about $339K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and productivity has risen 3.5% a year.
That works out to $27K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.3M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
